abstract: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) plays a pivotal role in tumor metastasis initiation. Although emerging evidence suggests that Tensin-1 (TNS1) contributes to tumor metastasis, its precise function in EMT during lung cancer progression and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify that TNS1 is upregulated in a TGFβ-induced EMT cell model. Functional studies demonstrate that TNS1 knockdown significantly attenuates both TGFβ- and hypoxia-induced EMT, highlighting its critical role in this process. Furthermore, TNS1 overexpression promotes EMT and enhances the metastatic potential of lung cancer cells in vitro and in vivo, while knockdown of TNS1 exhibits opposite effects. Mechanistically, TNS1 upregulation during TGFβ- mediated EMT is found to be transcriptionally regulated by ZEB1 and SMAD3. Notably, elevated TNS1 levels stabilizes ZEB1 through their interaction, thereby suppressing its ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation. Collectively, these findings uncover a positive feedback loop between TNS1 and ZEB1 that amplifies TGFβ-induced EMT and promotes lung cancer metastasis.

Materials and methods
Cell culture and establishment of EMT model
Human lung cancer cells cell lines A549 and H1299, alongside human CRC cell lines HCT116 and SW480, were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM). Human lung cancer cell lines H358, PC9, and H1975 were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium. All media were supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin. Cells were incubated at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO
2
atmosphere. To induce a mesenchymal-like phenotype via TGFβ, A549 and H358 cells were cultured in their respective standard growth media supplemented with 5 ng/mL of TGFβ1 (PeproTech, #100-21 C), whereas H1299, HCT116, and SW480 cells were cultured in medium supplemented with 1% (v/v) FBS and 10 ng/mL of TGFβ1. For hypoxia-mediated mesenchymal-like phenotype, A549, H358, H1299, HCT116, and SW480 cells were cultured in their standard growth media within a three-gas incubator at 37°C supplemented with 5% CO
2
and 2% O
2
. All cells were validated by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling and routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination using RT-qPCR analysis.
Plasmid constructs
The TNS1 expression plasmid was constructed by cloning the coding sequence of human TNS1 into the pCDH-CMV-MCS-EF1-Puro vector (System Biosciences). The coding sequences of human ZEB1 and SMAD3 were cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to generate ZEB1- and SMAD3-overexpressing plasmids. For gene knockdown, two independent short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting each gene (
FSTL1
,
LAMC2
,
TNS1
,
SMAD3
, or
ZEB1
) were cloned into the pLKO.1 lentiviral vector, with non-targeting shRNA (Scr) serving as the scramble control. Luciferase reporter constructs were generated by cloning two distinct
TNS1
promoter fragments (−2000/+200 bp or −500/+200 bp relative to transcription start site, TSS) into the pGL3-basic firefly luciferase vector. TNS1-binding-deficient mutants were constructed by QuikChange II Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (Agilent, #200524, USA). All primer sequences used in this study were listed in Supplementary Data
5
.
Lentivirus production and infection
HEK293T cells were co-transfected with gene-specific overexpression, knockdown, or mutant plasmids, the envelope plasmid pMD2.G, and the packaging plasmid psPAX2 at a ratio of 5:2:3 (vector: pMD2.G: psPAX2) using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, #11668019, USA). Supernatants were collected at 24, 48, and 72 h post-transfection, pooled, and centrifuged (3000 rpm, 10 min, 4 °C) to remove cellular debris. Clarified supernatant was aliquoted and stored at −80 °C. For lentivirus infection, cells were incubated overnight with lentivirus particles supplemented with 10 μg/mL of polybrene (Solarbio, #H8761). After a 48-h infection, stable cells were selected using 2 μg/mL puromycin (Thermo, #A1113802, USA) for 48 h, followed by maintenance in 1 μg/mL puromycin for 7 days.
The quantitative proteomics analysis
Cultured cells (
n
= 3 per group) were homogenized in lysis buffer (8 M urea, 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5). Protein mixtures were digested overnight with sequencing-grade modified trypsin (Promega, #V5113, USA) at a 1:50 (w/w) enzyme-to-protein ratio as previously described
48
. Equal amounts of peptides were reconstituted in 100 mM HEPES (pH 8.5) and labeled using TMT 6-plex reagents according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Labeled peptides were then fractionated by high-pH reversed-phase HPLC as described in a previous study
49
. Peptide samples (500 ng each) were reconstituted in 0.1% FA/H2O and subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis using an Easy-nLC 2000 HPLC system coupled with an Orbitrap ExplorisTM 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The HPLC and mass spectrometer parameters were done as previously described
49
. For protein identification and quantification, the raw MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer™ 2.4 with the Sequest HT engine, utilizing the Human_SwissProt database appended with known contaminants.
Bioinformatics analysis of the quantitative proteome
Proteomic data were processed using R (version 4.3.0). Differential protein analyses were conducted via two-sided Student’s
t
-test. Proteins meeting criteria of
p
< 0.05 and absolute fold-change > 1.2 or < 0.83 were classified as differentially expressed (up or downregulated). GO enrichment analysis of these proteins was performed using the clusterProfiler R package. Additionally, the networks for TNS1-regulated DEPs were constructed using the STRING and visualized in Cytoscape (v3.10.1). Total quantified protein in A549 cells treated/untreated with TGFβ were assessed using GSEA (V4.2.3) software for enrichment map analysis. Significantly enriched gene sets (
p
< 0.05, FDR < 0.25) were visualized as enrichment maps in Cytoscape using the EnrichmentMap 3.3. Nodes represented gene sets sized by member count and colored by Normalized Enrichment Score (NES; red: positive NES, blue: negative NES). Gene sets were organized into groups and scaled based on shared components (edge > 0.5) and their similarity (size).
Kaplan–Meier survival analysis
Survival analysis was conducted using Kaplan–Meier methodology with the median expression level of TNS1 serving as the cutoff to stratify patients into high- and low-expression cohorts. Proteomic data were acquired from ProteomeXchange (accession: PXD020548
50
) and processed by calculating median expression values in Microsoft Excel, followed by survival curve generation using the Wei Sheng Xin online platform (
https://www.bioinformatics.com.cn/plot_basic_kaplan_meier_survival_curve_plot_040
). Additional datasets were analyzed through the BEST bioinformatics platform (
https://rookieutopia.com/app_direct/BEST/
), which provides automated data processing and visualization pipelines. The analyzed datasets included transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA_LUSC and TCGA_LUAD) and microarray datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (
GSE68465
,
GSE72094
,
GSE30219
,
GSE3141
,
GSE63459
,
GSE50081
, and
GSE41271
).
Western blot assay
Cells were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, #P0013B, China) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, #PPC1010, Switzerland), and protein concentration was determined using the BCA assay kit (Beyotime, #P0009, China). Equal protein quantities were electrophoresed on either 8% or 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (GE #10600021, USA) at 300 mA constant current. Membranes were subsequently blocked in 5% non-fat milk/0.1% TBST for 2 h at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibody at 4 °C. After three 10-min TBST washes, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody for 1.5 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membranes were incubated with an enhanced chemiluminescence horseradish peroxidase (HRP) substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific #34076, USA). After an additional three rinses in 0.1% TBST, chemiluminescent signal visualization was performed using ChemiDoc XRS+ System (Bio-Rad, USA). Uncropped Western blot results were provided in Supplementary Fig.
5
.
RNA isolation and RT-qPCR assay
Total RNAs were isolated using RNAiso Plus reagent (TaKaRa, #9109), and 1 μg of RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the PrimeScript
TM
RT reagent kit (TaKaRa, #RR047A) according to manufacturer’s protocols. Subsequently, quantitative PCR amplification was performed in technical triplicates using TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (TaKaRa, #RR820A) according to manufacturer specifications using a QuantStudio 6 Operating Software (Life Technologies). Quantitative analysis was performed using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method with Ct values normalized to human actin/GAPDH. All samples were analyzed in triplicates. Primer sequences are detailed in Supplementary Data
5
.
Cell migration and invasion assays
In invasion assay, Transwell chambers (Falcon, #FAL-353097) were coated with Matrigel (Corning, #356231, USA) diluted 1:8 in serum-free DMEM at 37 °C for 30 min. Uncoated chambers were used for migration assays. Cells were suspended in RPMI-1640/DMEM medium containing 5% BSA. Subsequently, 200 µL suspension of 30,000–50,000 cells was seeded into the top chamber, with 600 μL complete growth medium serving as a chemoattractant in the lower chamber. Following 24-h incubation at 37 °C in 5% CO
2
, non-migrated cells were removed from the upper surface with cotton swabs. Transmigrated cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min, and then stained with 0.5% crystal violet solution (Beyotime, #C0121) for 20 min, and imaged at 100× magnification. Migrated cells were quantified using ImageJ automated cell counting. Data visualization and statistical analysis utilized GraphPad Prism v.9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).
Cell proliferation assay
Cell proliferation was assessed using both MTT and colony formation assays. For the MTT assay, 1000 cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated for specified durations (1, 3, 5, 7 day). Following the addition of 20 μL 5 mg/mL MTT solution (Sigma, #M5655) to the medium of each well, the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 4 h in the dark. Absorbance at 490 nm was then measured using a BioTek microplate reader. For the colony formation assay, 1500 cells were seeded into each well of 6-well plate and cultured for 10 days in a humidified 5% CO
2
incubator, with medium replacement every 3 days. Cell colonies were subsequently fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min and stained with 0.5% crystal violet solution (Beyotime, #C0121) for 20 min, quantified by manual counting of scanned images using ImageJ (v1.53), and statistically analyzed with GraphPad Prism v.9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).
Immunoprecipitation (IP) assay
Cells were lysed in ice-cold IP buffer (150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5% Triton ×-100, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche) for 20 min on ice. Following centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was incubated with the ZEB1 antibody (Proteintech, #21544-1-AP), TNS1 antibody (Sigma, #SAB4200283), or an equivalent amount of IgG at 4 °C overnight. Protein A/G-Sepharose beads (Millipore, USA) were pre-blocked with 5% BSA overnight, and subsequently incubated with the antibody-supernatant mixture at 4 °C for 4 h. After washing three times with wash buffer (150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.1% Triton ×-100, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5), the immunoprecipitated proteins were eluted with 2 × SDS loading buffer by boiling at 95 °C for 10 min and further subjected to Western blot.
For Flag-tagged protein immunoprecipitation, cells stably expressing Flag-tagged constructs (full-length, truncated, or mutant TNS1) or empty vector controls were lysed as above. Cleared lysates were incubated with ANTI-FLAG
®
M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma #A2220) under rotational agitation at 4 °C for 4 h. Beads were washed three times with wash buffer, and bound proteins were eluted by boiling in 2 × SDS loading buffer (95 °C, 10 min) prior to Western blot analysis.
Cytosolic and nuclear fractionation protocol
To obtain cytosolic fractions, cells were disrupted using hypotonic lysis buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 5 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.5% NP-40) for 10 min on ice. Cellular debris was subsequently pelleted by centrifugation at 5000 ×
g
for 5 min. Nuclei were separated from the cytoplasmic supernatants and washed once with hypotonic buffer. The washed nuclear pellets were then lysed in RIPA buffer (Beyotime, #P0013B) for 15 min on ice. Following lysis, nuclear fractions were isolated by centrifugation at 16,000 ×
g
for 10 min. Cytosolic and nuclear fractions were respectively validated using GAPDH and Lamin A/C as compartment-specific markers.
Ubiquitination assay
Cells transfected with 2 µg of HA-ubiquitin plasmid (Addgene #18712) were harvested 48 h post-transfection. Cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, detached by scraping in 2 mL PBS per 10-cm dish, and pelleted by centrifugation at 500 ×
g
for 5 min at 4 °C. Cell pellets were resuspended in IP buffer for subsequent immunoprecipitation (as previously defined).
Luciferase reporter assay
Luciferase reporter assay was conducted using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System (Promega, #E2920) according to manufacturers’ instructions. Briefly, the pGL3-basic vector containing
TNS1
promoter region (−2000/+200 bp or −500/+200 bp relative to TSS), pcDNA3.1 vector containing Smad3 coding sequence and ZEB1 coding sequence or an empty vector, and a renilla luciferase plasmid were co-transfected into 293T cells using lipofectamine 2000 at a ratio of 2: 2: 1. After 24 h, 1 × 10
4
transfected cells were seeded into 96-well plates and incubated for 24 h. Luciferase reporter activity was measured by the Dual-Glo luciferase assay reagents on a PE microplate reader. Each sample was performed in triplicates.
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
ChIP assay was performed using the SimpleChIP Plus Enzymatic Chromatin IP kit (Agarose beads) (Cell Signaling Technology, #9004) according to manufacturer guidelines with modifications. A549 cells were treated with TGFβ (10 ng/mL) or equal volume of PBS (Vehicle control) for 16 h. Subsequently, 1 × 10
7
cells were fixed by 1% formaldehyde for 10 min and terminated by adding 0.125 M glycine for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were washed twice with PBS, pelleted by centrifugation at 2000 ×
g
for 5 min. Nuclei were isolated and chromatin fragmented by enzymatic digestion with 0.5 μL Micrococcal Nuclease (Cell Signaling Technology, #10011) at 37 °C for 20 min, followed by sonication. Fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C with anti-Smad3 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, #9523), ZEB1 antibody (Proteintech, #21544-1-AP), or rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling Technology, #2729). Antibody-chromatin complexes were captured with ChIP-Grade Protein G Agarose Beads (Cell Signaling Technology, #9007) and washed in accordance with the protocol described. Next, the antibody-chromatin complex was decrosslinked by Proteinase K at 67 °C for 2 h, then DNA was purified using the Takara MiniBEST DNA Fragment Purification kit (Takara, #9761). Enrichment at target loci was quantified by qPCR analysis. Primer sequences were depicted in Supplementary Data
5
.
Animal experiments
All animal studies were conducted in accordance with the protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Approval No. 20221228003) and complied with all relevant ethical regulations. Four- to six-week-old female BALB/c nude mice (
n
= 6 per group) were purchased from Gempharmatech (Jiangsu, China) and randomly assigned to either vehicle control (Vec) or TNS1 overexpression (TNS1) groups. Mice were housed under specific-pathogen-free conditions in individually ventilated cages with a 12-h light–dark cycle, ambient temperature of 21 ± 1 °C, and 55–70% of humidity. Tumor volume was strictly maintained below the committee-approved limit of 2000 mm
3
throughout the study. To establish metastasis models, mice received intracardiac injections of 1 × 10⁵ cells in 100 μL PBS. Four weeks post-injection, bioluminescence imaging was performed using an IVIS SpectrumCT system (Revvity, USA) at 10 min after intraperitoneal administration of 100 µL D-luciferin (15 mg/mL, Promega, USA), and images were analyzed with Living Image 4.8.2 software (Caliper Life Sciences, USA). Following imaging, mice were sacrificed by rapid cervical dislocation, and no animals were excluded from the analysis. Bone, brain, lung, and liver tissues were harvested, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, cleared in xylene, and embedded in paraffin. Tissue sections (4–5 μm thickness) were mounted on glass slides, deparaffinized, and stained with hematoxylin (5 min) and eosin (1 min) using standard protocols.

Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism v.9.0 software (GraphPad, USA). Comparisons between two groups were analyzed by two-tailed unpaired Student’s
t
-test was employed for comparisons between two groups, and one-way ANOVA was used for multi-group comparisons. All experiments were independently repeated at least three times. Statistical significance was defined as
p
< 0.05 with the following notation: *
p
< 0.05, **
p
< 0.01, and ***
p
< 0.001.

Introduction
Lung cancer is the second most common frequently diagnosed malignancy and the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately 2.2 million new cases and 1.8 million deaths annually
1
. Metastasis constitutes a major determinant of poor prognosis in lung cancer patients, involving a multiple cascade whereby malignant cells dissociate from the primary tumor, intravasate into lymphatic and circulatory systems, disseminate systemically, and ultimately establish secondary lesions at distant sites
2
,
3
. This metastatic progression is critically dependent on epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a fundamental cellular reprogramming that enables migratory and invasive capabilities. EMT encompasses a dynamic phenotypic transformation marked by profound cytoskeletal remodeling, dissolution of epithelial cell-cell junctions, and acquisition of mesenchymal characteristics
4
. Core EMT transcription factors, including ZEB1/2, SNAIL, and SLUG, orchestrate this process by modulating downstream effector genes
5
. Multiple extracellular cues, particularly TGFβ signaling and hypoxia stress, have been well-documented in the induction and maintenance of EMT
6
,
7
. Notably, EMT progression is tightly regulated through intricate feedback mechanisms. A prototypical example is the reciprocal negative feedback between ZEB1 and miR-200 family members, which is critical for cellular plasticity and EMT process of cancer cells
8
.
ZEB1 is a pivotal EMT transcription factor and contains two C2H2-type zinc finger clusters that specifically recognize and bind to CACCT(G) E-box-like promoter elements in target genes
9
. With a relatively short half-life of approximately 3 h, ZEB1 protein levels are tightly controlled through ubiquitin/proteasome-mediated degradation
10
. Substantial clinical evidence demonstrates that high ZEB1 expression correlates with adverse clinical outcomes, including poor prognosis, chemotherapy resistance, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and metastatic progression
11
. ZEB1 is reported to regulate the expression of target genes via modulating DNA methylation and histone modification or recruiting co-suppressors and co-activators. For example, Postigo et al. disclosed that ZEB1 forms functional complexes with co-activators including Smad proteins, p300, and P/CAF to promote expression of TGFβ-responsive genes
12
. Similarly, Comijn et al. revealed that ZEB1 directly binds to the
CDH1
promoter, recruiting transcriptional repressor to suppress E-cadherin expression
13
.
TNS1 is a focal adhesion protein that anchors actin cytoskeletons to integrin receptors, playing important roles in diverse cellular processes, including cell adhesion, polarization, migration, and invasion
14
. As a key component of focal adhesions, TNS1 facilitates the recruitment of tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins and SH2 domain-containing proteins, thereby functioning as a dynamic platform for the assembly and disassembly of signaling transduction complexes. During EMT process, migrating mesenchymal-like cells form nascent adhesions at the leading edge while dissembling and recycling rear adhesions through endocytosis
15
. Numerous scaffold and signaling proteins, including paxillin, vinculin, focal adhesion kinase, and Src family kinases, are localized at focal adhesions
16
. Thus, focal adhesions may function as signaling nodes that integrate extracellular cues with intracellular EMT signaling pathways. Although TGFβ signaling has been shown to upregulate both TNS1 protein expression and phosphorylation status
17
,
18
, the functional significance of TNS1 in EMT progression and its molecular mechanisms remain elusive.
In this study, we employed quantitative proteomic profiling to identify TNS1 as one of the most significantly upregulated proteins in TGFβ-treated lung cancer cells. Clinical correlation analysis revealed that elevated TNS1 expression in metastatic lesions compared to primary lung tumors, with higher TNS1 levels associated with poorer patient prognosis. Using gain- and loss-of-function approaches, we demonstrated that TNS1 promotes EMT and metastasis in both in vitro and in vivo models of lung cancer. Mechanistic investigations established that TGFβ-induced TNS1 upregulation is mediated through transcriptional activation by ZEB1 and SMAD3. Notably, we discovered that TNS1 reciprocally stabilizes ZEB1 protein through their interaction, thereby protecting ZEB1 from ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation. Therefore, these findings delineate a positive feedback regulatory circuit between TNS1 and ZEB1 that promotes EMT progression in lung cancer cells.
Results
Identification of differentially expressed proteins during TGFβ-induced EMT
To identify key mediators of EMT, we established a TGFβ-induced EMT model using A549 lung cancer cells and performed TMT-labeled quantitative proteomic analyses comparing untreated and TGFβ-treated cells (Fig.
1A
). Successful EMT induction was confirmed by morphological transition to a fibroblast-like phenotype (Fig.
1B
), and characteristic molecular changes, including the downregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin and the upregulation of mesenchymal makers N-cadherin and vimentin (Fig.
1C
), consistent with previous reports
19
,
20
. Proteomic profiling quantified 7401 proteins, with 390 showing significant differential expression following TGFβ treatment (Fig.
1D
and Supplementary Data
2
). Bioinformatics analyses revealed that these differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) are enriched in EMT-related pathways, including regulation of cell adhesion, regulation of cell migration, and cell-matrix adhesion (Supplementary Fig.
1
), validating the effective induction of EMT by TGFβ. Within Gene Ontology (GO) categories associated with cell migration and adhesion (Fig.
1E
, Left), FSTL1, LAMC2, TGFBI, and TNS1 exhibited the most significant upregulation in the TGFβ-treated group (Fig.
1E
, Right). TGFBI has been previously demonstrated to be highly expressed and play a key role in TGFβ-induced EMT
21
, whereas FSTL1, LAMC2, and TNS1 have not been reported to participate in EMT although they have potential to regulate metastasis
22
–
24
. Thus, TNS1, LAMC2, and FSTL1 were investigated in this study.

TNS1 knockdown impairs TGFβ/hypoxia-induced EMT in lung cancer cells
To assess the functional contribution of TNS1, LAMC2, and FSTL1 to EMT progression, we employed loss-of-function approaches using shRNA-mediated stable knockdown in A549 cells. As anticipated, TGFβ treatment significantly reduced E-cadherin expression while enhancing N-cadherin and vimentin levels (Fig.
2A–C
). Although the expression of TNS1, LAMC2, and FSTL1 were obviously induced by TGFβ stimulation, only TNS1 depletion effectively impaired TGFβ-induced EMT marker changes (Fig.
2A–C
), indicating TNS1 as the important mediator of TGFβ-driven EMT. Moreover, TNS1 knockdown abrogated TGFβ-induced mesenchymal morphological transition (Fig.
2D
).

As hypoxia is another well-established trigger of EMT process
25
, we extended our investigation in hypoxia-induced EMT model. Hypoxia treatment similarly upregulated TNS1 expression in A549 cells, and TNS1 knockdown attenuated both hypoxia-induced EMT marker alternations (Fig.
2E
) and morphological changes (Fig.
2F
). To evaluate broader relevance of these findings, we examined four additional cancer cell lines (lung cancer cells: H1299 and H358; colorectal cancer (CRC) cells: SW480 and HCT116), which were chosen because of their TGFβ responsiveness and EMT capacity (Fig.

). Across all models, TGFβ treatment consistently upregulated vimentin expression and downregulated E-cadherin levels (Fig.

TNS1 is a ZEB1 and SMAD3-regulated target in TGFβ signaling
Given the significant upregulation of
TNS1
mRNA during TGFβ- and hypoxia-induced EMT (Figs.

and

and Supplementary Data

TNS1

To test this, we examined the effects of ZEB1 or SMAD3 on TNS1 expression in multiple lung cancer cell lines. The results showed that ectopic overexpression of either ZEB1 or SMAD3 consistently upregulated TNS1 expression at both protein and mRNA levels (Fig.
3B–E
). Conversely, shRNA-mediated depletion of ZEB1 or SMAD3 attenuated TGFβ-induced TNS1 upregulation (Fig.
3F–I
).

Discussion
EMT process is precisely controlled by complex regulatory networks comprising transcription factors and their downstream effectors. While numerous EMT regulators have been identified, our understanding of this critical biological program remains incomplete. Building upon our previous discovery of a circular RNA regulating TGFβ-induced EMT
33
, we performed comprehensive quantitative proteomic profiling to identify novel components of the TGFβ-induced EMT program. From this analysis, we identified three metastasis-associated proteins (FSTL1, LAMC2, and TNS1) that exhibited dose- and time-dependent upregulation in response to TGFβ stimulation (Fig.
1G–J
). Functional validation revealed that only TNS1 depletion effectively impaired TGFβ-induced EMT in lung cancer cells, as evidenced by preserved epithelial morphology and marker expression (Fig.
2A and D
). These findings establish TNS1 as a previously unrecognized yet essential regulator of EMT.
Given that TGFβ treatment simultaneously induced EMT and upregulated
TNS1
mRNA expression (Fig.
1
), together with the well-documented involvement of specific transcription factors in EMT regulation
5
, we speculated that core EMT transcription factors associated with TGFβ and hypoxia signaling pathways control TNS1 expression. Our systematic investigation identified ZEB1 and SMAD3 as the key transcriptional regulators of TNS1, supported by the existence of predicted binding sites within the
TNS1
promoter region (Fig.
3A
), direct binding of ZEB1 and SMAD3 to the
TNS1
promoter (Fig.
3J–O
), and a serial of in vitro experimental results: ectopic expression of either ZEB1 or SMAD3 significantly increased
TNS1
mRNA and protein levels (Fig.
3B–E
) and enhanced
TNS1
promoter-driven luciferase expression (Fig.
3J and K
), whereas depletion of either factor impaired TGFβ-mediated TNS1 upregulation (Fig.
3F–I
). This study provides the first demonstration that TGFβ induces
TNS1
transcription by ZEB1 and SMAD3.
Accumulating evidence indicates that TNS1 exhibits context-dependent roles in tumor biology, with multiple studies demonstrating its pro-tumorigenic functions across malignancies. For example, TNS1 knockout suppresses breast cancer cell growth and migration by impairing adhesion dynamics
23
. Similarly, TNS1 depletion inhibits proliferative capacity and invadopodia formation in liver cancer cells
34
. Moreover, elevated TNS1 expression correlates with poor overall survival in CRC patients, and its knockdown reduces CRC cell proliferation and invasiveness
29
. Although TNS1 has been reported to promote migration and invasion in A549 and H460 lung cancer cells by activating Akt/mTOR/RhoA signaling axis
35
, paradoxically, TNS1 overexpression was found to suppress proliferative and invasive capacity in brain-adapted NSCLC sublines (BrM-A549 and BrM-H1915)
36
. These opposing phenotypic effects likely arise from fundamental differences in cellular context (e.g., primary vs. brain-adapted sublines). Our results demonstrate that TNS1 overexpression significantly enhances migratory capacity and invasive potential in both A549 and H1299 cells without significant effect on proliferative activity, whereas TNS1 depletion attenuates these malignant properties in A549 and H1975 cells (Fig.
5A–F
and Supplementary Fig.
3
). Furthermore, TNS1 promotes lung cancer metastasis in xenograft mouse models (Fig.
5G–I
). Clinical correlation studies indicate that high TNS1 expression correlates with worse survival in lung cancer patients (Fig.
4B
and Supplementary Fig.
2
). These findings collectively establish TNS1’s pro-metastatic role in lung cancer progression.
EMT programs are tightly regulated through intricate positive and negative feedback mechanisms. The well-established examples are reciprocal regulatory loops between EMT-related transcriptional factors and microRNAs, such as the double-negative feedback between ZEB1 with miR-200 family
37
, SNAIL-mediated repression of miR-34a
38
, and TWIST1 suppression of miR-186
39
. Additionally, EMT-related transcriptional factors also form protein-protein feedback networks that modulate EMT progression. For instance, Grainyhead-like-2 (GRHL2) and ZEB1 establish a mutually antagonistic relationship that control EMT dynamics in breast cancer
40
, while myocardin (MYOCD) forms a positive feedback loop with SMAD3/SMAD4 to promote TGFβ-induced EMT and metastasis in NSCLC
41
. In this study, we revealed a regulatory axis in this network: TGFβ signaling activates
TNS1
transcription through ZEB1 and SMAD3 (Figs.
3
and
8H
), and upregulated TNS1 protein interacts with and stabilizes ZEB1 by preventing its ubiquitin-mediated degradation (Figs.
6
–
8
), thereby establishing a feed-forward loop that potentiates TGFβ-induced EMT in lung cancer. This finding expands the known functions of TNS1, a focal adhesion scaffold protein previously shown to bind the tumor suppressor DLC1 via its C-terminal SH2/PTB domains, inhibiting DLC1 RhoGAP activity
42
, and to require PP1α and DLC1 to regulate cell polarization and invasion
43
. We demonstrate that TNS1’s SH2 domain mediates ZEB1 stability (Figs.
7
and
8
), revealing previously unrecognized mechanism by which TNS1 promotes EMT and metastasis.
As a key regulator of EMT, ZEB1 plays a pivotal role in driving tumor progression and metastasis
44
. Growing evidence indicates that ZEB1’s stability and transcriptional activity are dynamically regulated through post-translational modifications and protein-protein interactions. For example, ATM-mediated phosphorylation enhances ZEB1 stability during DNA damage responses
45
. In triple-negative breast cancer, CHFR promotes ZEB1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation
46
. Additionally, CASP8AP2 antagonizes SIAH1/FBXO45-mediated ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of ZEB1, with CASP8AP2 depletion leading to ZEB1 destabilization and EMT
47
. Our findings extend this regulatory paradigm by identifying TNS1 as a potential stabilizer of ZEB1 protein through inhibiting its proteasomal degradation (Fig.
8
). However, the exact molecular mechanism of TNS1-mediated ZEB1 stabilization require further investigation. We propose two potential mechanisms. One is competitive protection model: The TNS1-ZEB1 interaction may sterically hinder ZEB1’s recognition by specific E3 ligases or recruit deubiquitinating enzymes to modulate ZEB1’s ubiquitination. The other is ubiquitin shielding model: TNS1 binding to ubiquitinated ZEB1 could mask ZEB1 from 26S proteasome recognition or interfere with K48-linked polyubiquitin chain elongation. These possibilities will be systematically investigated in future studies through comprehensive biochemical and proteomic approaches.
In summary, TNS1 was identified as a critical molecular effector in TGFβ-induced EMT in lung cancer. TNS1 depletion markedly attenuated TGFβ/hypoxia-induced EMT progression, while TNS1 overexpression significantly enhances EMT and metastasis. Mechanistically, TNS1 expression is transcriptionally activated by ZEB1 and SMAD3 following TGFβ stimulation, and the upregulated TNS1 physically interacts with and stabilizes ZEB1 protein. Therefore, our findings elucidate a TNS1/ZEB1 positive feedback loop that amplify and sustains EMT activation, ultimately driving lung cancer metastasis.
Materials and methods
Cell culture and establishment of EMT model
Human lung cancer cells cell lines A549 and H1299, alongside human CRC cell lines HCT116 and SW480, were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM). Human lung cancer cell lines H358, PC9, and H1975 were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium. All media were supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin. Cells were incubated at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO
2
atmosphere. To induce a mesenchymal-like phenotype via TGFβ, A549 and H358 cells were cultured in their respective standard growth media supplemented with 5 ng/mL of TGFβ1 (PeproTech, #100-21 C), whereas H1299, HCT116, and SW480 cells were cultured in medium supplemented with 1% (v/v) FBS and 10 ng/mL of TGFβ1. For hypoxia-mediated mesenchymal-like phenotype, A549, H358, H1299, HCT116, and SW480 cells were cultured in their standard growth media within a three-gas incubator at 37°C supplemented with 5% CO
2
and 2% O
2
. All cells were validated by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling and routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination using RT-qPCR analysis.
Plasmid constructs
The TNS1 expression plasmid was constructed by cloning the coding sequence of human TNS1 into the pCDH-CMV-MCS-EF1-Puro vector (System Biosciences). The coding sequences of human ZEB1 and SMAD3 were cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to generate ZEB1- and SMAD3-overexpressing plasmids. For gene knockdown, two independent short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting each gene (
FSTL1
,
LAMC2
,
TNS1
,
SMAD3
, or
ZEB1
) were cloned into the pLKO.1 lentiviral vector, with non-targeting shRNA (Scr) serving as the scramble control. Luciferase reporter constructs were generated by cloning two distinct
TNS1
promoter fragments (−2000/+200 bp or −500/+200 bp relative to transcription start site, TSS) into the pGL3-basic firefly luciferase vector. TNS1-binding-deficient mutants were constructed by QuikChange II Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (Agilent, #200524, USA). All primer sequences used in this study were listed in Supplementary Data
5
.
Lentivirus production and infection
HEK293T cells were co-transfected with gene-specific overexpression, knockdown, or mutant plasmids, the envelope plasmid pMD2.G, and the packaging plasmid psPAX2 at a ratio of 5:2:3 (vector: pMD2.G: psPAX2) using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, #11668019, USA). Supernatants were collected at 24, 48, and 72 h post-transfection, pooled, and centrifuged (3000 rpm, 10 min, 4 °C) to remove cellular debris. Clarified supernatant was aliquoted and stored at −80 °C. For lentivirus infection, cells were incubated overnight with lentivirus particles supplemented with 10 μg/mL of polybrene (Solarbio, #H8761). After a 48-h infection, stable cells were selected using 2 μg/mL puromycin (Thermo, #A1113802, USA) for 48 h, followed by maintenance in 1 μg/mL puromycin for 7 days.
The quantitative proteomics analysis
Cultured cells (
n
= 3 per group) were homogenized in lysis buffer (8 M urea, 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.5). Protein mixtures were digested overnight with sequencing-grade modified trypsin (Promega, #V5113, USA) at a 1:50 (w/w) enzyme-to-protein ratio as previously described
48
. Equal amounts of peptides were reconstituted in 100 mM HEPES (pH 8.5) and labeled using TMT 6-plex reagents according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Labeled peptides were then fractionated by high-pH reversed-phase HPLC as described in a previous study
49
. Peptide samples (500 ng each) were reconstituted in 0.1% FA/H2O and subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis using an Easy-nLC 2000 HPLC system coupled with an Orbitrap ExplorisTM 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The HPLC and mass spectrometer parameters were done as previously described
49
. For protein identification and quantification, the raw MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer™ 2.4 with the Sequest HT engine, utilizing the Human_SwissProt database appended with known contaminants.
Bioinformatics analysis of the quantitative proteome
Proteomic data were processed using R (version 4.3.0). Differential protein analyses were conducted via two-sided Student’s
t
-test. Proteins meeting criteria of
p
< 0.05 and absolute fold-change > 1.2 or < 0.83 were classified as differentially expressed (up or downregulated). GO enrichment analysis of these proteins was performed using the clusterProfiler R package. Additionally, the networks for TNS1-regulated DEPs were constructed using the STRING and visualized in Cytoscape (v3.10.1). Total quantified protein in A549 cells treated/untreated with TGFβ were assessed using GSEA (V4.2.3) software for enrichment map analysis. Significantly enriched gene sets (
p
< 0.05, FDR < 0.25) were visualized as enrichment maps in Cytoscape using the EnrichmentMap 3.3. Nodes represented gene sets sized by member count and colored by Normalized Enrichment Score (NES; red: positive NES, blue: negative NES). Gene sets were organized into groups and scaled based on shared components (edge > 0.5) and their similarity (size).
Kaplan–Meier survival analysis
Survival analysis was conducted using Kaplan–Meier methodology with the median expression level of TNS1 serving as the cutoff to stratify patients into high- and low-expression cohorts. Proteomic data were acquired from ProteomeXchange (accession: PXD020548
50
) and processed by calculating median expression values in Microsoft Excel, followed by survival curve generation using the Wei Sheng Xin online platform (
https://www.bioinformatics.com.cn/plot_basic_kaplan_meier_survival_curve_plot_040
). Additional datasets were analyzed through the BEST bioinformatics platform (
https://rookieutopia.com/app_direct/BEST/
), which provides automated data processing and visualization pipelines. The analyzed datasets included transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA_LUSC and TCGA_LUAD) and microarray datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (
GSE68465
,
GSE72094
,
GSE30219
,
GSE3141
,

GSE50081
, and
GSE41271

Western blot assay
Cells were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, #P0013B, China) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, #PPC1010, Switzerland), and protein concentration was determined using the BCA assay kit (Beyotime, #P0009, China). Equal protein quantities were electrophoresed on either 8% or 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (GE #10600021, USA) at 300 mA constant current. Membranes were subsequently blocked in 5% non-fat milk/0.1% TBST for 2 h at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibody at 4 °C. After three 10-min TBST washes, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody for 1.5 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membranes were incubated with an enhanced chemiluminescence horseradish peroxidase (HRP) substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific #34076, USA). After an additional three rinses in 0.1% TBST, chemiluminescent signal visualization was performed using ChemiDoc XRS+ System (Bio-Rad, USA). Uncropped Western blot results were provided in Supplementary Fig.
5
.
RNA isolation and RT-qPCR assay
Total RNAs were isolated using RNAiso Plus reagent (TaKaRa, #9109), and 1 μg of RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the PrimeScript
TM
RT reagent kit (TaKaRa, #RR047A) according to manufacturer’s protocols. Subsequently, quantitative PCR amplification was performed in technical triplicates using TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (TaKaRa, #RR820A) according to manufacturer specifications using a QuantStudio 6 Operating Software (Life Technologies). Quantitative analysis was performed using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method with Ct values normalized to human actin/GAPDH. All samples were analyzed in triplicates. Primer sequences are detailed in Supplementary Data
5
.
Cell migration and invasion assays
In invasion assay, Transwell chambers (Falcon, #FAL-353097) were coated with Matrigel (Corning, #356231, USA) diluted 1:8 in serum-free DMEM at 37 °C for 30 min. Uncoated chambers were used for migration assays. Cells were suspended in RPMI-1640/DMEM medium containing 5% BSA. Subsequently, 200 µL suspension of 30,000–50,000 cells was seeded into the top chamber, with 600 μL complete growth medium serving as a chemoattractant in the lower chamber. Following 24-h incubation at 37 °C in 5% CO
2
, non-migrated cells were removed from the upper surface with cotton swabs. Transmigrated cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min, and then stained with 0.5% crystal violet solution (Beyotime, #C0121) for 20 min, and imaged at 100× magnification. Migrated cells were quantified using ImageJ automated cell counting. Data visualization and statistical analysis utilized GraphPad Prism v.9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).
Cell proliferation assay
Cell proliferation was assessed using both MTT and colony formation assays. For the MTT assay, 1000 cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated for specified durations (1, 3, 5, 7 day). Following the addition of 20 μL 5 mg/mL MTT solution (Sigma, #M5655) to the medium of each well, the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 4 h in the dark. Absorbance at 490 nm was then measured using a BioTek microplate reader. For the colony formation assay, 1500 cells were seeded into each well of 6-well plate and cultured for 10 days in a humidified 5% CO
2
incubator, with medium replacement every 3 days. Cell colonies were subsequently fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min and stained with 0.5% crystal violet solution (Beyotime, #C0121) for 20 min, quantified by manual counting of scanned images using ImageJ (v1.53), and statistically analyzed with GraphPad Prism v.9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).
Immunoprecipitation (IP) assay
Cells were lysed in ice-cold IP buffer (150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5% Triton ×-100, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche) for 20 min on ice. Following centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was incubated with the ZEB1 antibody (Proteintech, #21544-1-AP), TNS1 antibody (Sigma, #SAB4200283), or an equivalent amount of IgG at 4 °C overnight. Protein A/G-Sepharose beads (Millipore, USA) were pre-blocked with 5% BSA overnight, and subsequently incubated with the antibody-supernatant mixture at 4 °C for 4 h. After washing three times with wash buffer (150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.1% Triton ×-100, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5), the immunoprecipitated proteins were eluted with 2 × SDS loading buffer by boiling at 95 °C for 10 min and further subjected to Western blot.
For Flag-tagged protein immunoprecipitation, cells stably expressing Flag-tagged constructs (full-length, truncated, or mutant TNS1) or empty vector controls were lysed as above. Cleared lysates were incubated with ANTI-FLAG
®
M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma #A2220) under rotational agitation at 4 °C for 4 h. Beads were washed three times with wash buffer, and bound proteins were eluted by boiling in 2 × SDS loading buffer (95 °C, 10 min) prior to Western blot analysis.
Cytosolic and nuclear fractionation protocol
To obtain cytosolic fractions, cells were disrupted using hypotonic lysis buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 5 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.5% NP-40) for 10 min on ice. Cellular debris was subsequently pelleted by centrifugation at 5000 ×
g
for 5 min. Nuclei were separated from the cytoplasmic supernatants and washed once with hypotonic buffer. The washed nuclear pellets were then lysed in RIPA buffer (Beyotime, #P0013B) for 15 min on ice. Following lysis, nuclear fractions were isolated by centrifugation at 16,000 ×
g
for 10 min. Cytosolic and nuclear fractions were respectively validated using GAPDH and Lamin A/C as compartment-specific markers.
Ubiquitination assay
Cells transfected with 2 µg of HA-ubiquitin plasmid (Addgene #18712) were harvested 48 h post-transfection. Cells were washed with ice-cold PBS, detached by scraping in 2 mL PBS per 10-cm dish, and pelleted by centrifugation at 500 ×
g
for 5 min at 4 °C. Cell pellets were resuspended in IP buffer for subsequent immunoprecipitation (as previously defined).
Luciferase reporter assay
Luciferase reporter assay was conducted using the Dual-Glo Luciferase Assay System (Promega, #E2920) according to manufacturers’ instructions. Briefly, the pGL3-basic vector containing
TNS1
promoter region (−2000/+200 bp or −500/+200 bp relative to TSS), pcDNA3.1 vector containing Smad3 coding sequence and ZEB1 coding sequence or an empty vector, and a renilla luciferase plasmid were co-transfected into 293T cells using lipofectamine 2000 at a ratio of 2: 2: 1. After 24 h, 1 × 10
4
transfected cells were seeded into 96-well plates and incubated for 24 h. Luciferase reporter activity was measured by the Dual-Glo luciferase assay reagents on a PE microplate reader. Each sample was performed in triplicates.
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay
ChIP assay was performed using the SimpleChIP Plus Enzymatic Chromatin IP kit (Agarose beads) (Cell Signaling Technology, #9004) according to manufacturer guidelines with modifications. A549 cells were treated with TGFβ (10 ng/mL) or equal volume of PBS (Vehicle control) for 16 h. Subsequently, 1 × 10
7
cells were fixed by 1% formaldehyde for 10 min and terminated by adding 0.125 M glycine for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were washed twice with PBS, pelleted by centrifugation at 2000 ×
g
for 5 min. Nuclei were isolated and chromatin fragmented by enzymatic digestion with 0.5 μL Micrococcal Nuclease (Cell Signaling Technology, #10011) at 37 °C for 20 min, followed by sonication. Fragmented chromatin was immunoprecipitated overnight at 4 °C with anti-Smad3 antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, #9523), ZEB1 antibody (Proteintech, #21544-1-AP), or rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling Technology, #2729). Antibody-chromatin complexes were captured with ChIP-Grade Protein G Agarose Beads (Cell Signaling Technology, #9007) and washed in accordance with the protocol described. Next, the antibody-chromatin complex was decrosslinked by Proteinase K at 67 °C for 2 h, then DNA was purified using the Takara MiniBEST DNA Fragment Purification kit (Takara, #9761). Enrichment at target loci was quantified by qPCR analysis. Primer sequences were depicted in Supplementary Data
5
.
Animal experiments
All animal studies were conducted in accordance with the protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Approval No. 20221228003) and complied with all relevant ethical regulations. Four- to six-week-old female BALB/c nude mice (
n
= 6 per group) were purchased from Gempharmatech (Jiangsu, China) and randomly assigned to either vehicle control (Vec) or TNS1 overexpression (TNS1) groups. Mice were housed under specific-pathogen-free conditions in individually ventilated cages with a 12-h light–dark cycle, ambient temperature of 21 ± 1 °C, and 55–70% of humidity. Tumor volume was strictly maintained below the committee-approved limit of 2000 mm
3
throughout the study. To establish metastasis models, mice received intracardiac injections of 1 × 10⁵ cells in 100 μL PBS. Four weeks post-injection, bioluminescence imaging was performed using an IVIS SpectrumCT system (Revvity, USA) at 10 min after intraperitoneal administration of 100 µL D-luciferin (15 mg/mL, Promega, USA), and images were analyzed with Living Image 4.8.2 software (Caliper Life Sciences, USA). Following imaging, mice were sacrificed by rapid cervical dislocation, and no animals were excluded from the analysis. Bone, brain, lung, and liver tissues were harvested, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, cleared in xylene, and embedded in paraffin. Tissue sections (4–5 μm thickness) were mounted on glass slides, deparaffinized, and stained with hematoxylin (5 min) and eosin (1 min) using standard protocols.

t
-test was employed for comparisons between two groups, and one-way ANOVA was used for multi-group comparisons. All experiments were independently repeated at least three times. Statistical significance was defined as
p
< 0.05 with the following notation: *
p

p
< 0.01, and ***
